title: The One Conversation Every Dating Couple Avoids
paragraphs:
The One Conversation Every Dating Couple Avoids
If You Can’t Talk About This Before Marriage, It Will Eventually Talk for You
There is a conversation almost every dating couple postpones.
Not because they don't know it matters.
But because they know it might change everything.
Talk about wedding colors, dream houses, future children, travel plans, and forever.
Yet beneath all the excitement sits one silent question neither wants to ask.
"Who are you... when everything beautiful disappears?"
That conversation is often delayed because love feels safer when mystery remains.
But Scripture never teaches us to build relationships on carefully edited versions of ourselves.
It teaches us to walk in light.
"But if we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin." (1 John 1:7)
The Greek word translated "walk" is περιπατῶμεν (peripatōmen).
It doesn't mean taking occasional spiritual steps.
It means a continuous way of life.
Many dating relationships survive on attraction.
Some survive because both people fear being alone.
But relationships that glorify Christ survive because two sinners choose truth over performance.
Because eventually every relationship reaches the place where masks become exhausting.
The spiritual dryness behind public worship.
Distance becomes loneliness while sharing the same bed.
Scripture introduces us to the very first human relationship.
"And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed." (Genesis 2:25)
The Hebrew word for "naked" is עֲרוּמִּים ('arummim).
This is not merely physical nakedness.
Within the literary context of Genesis, it represents complete openness.
The first response to sin was not violence.
The first relationship broken by sin immediately became a relationship built on concealment.
Today's fig leaves simply look different.
Saying "I'm okay" when your soul is collapsing.
Pretending purity while privately fighting temptation.
Acting spiritually mature while secretly doubting God.
Dating often becomes the art of presenting the most lovable version of ourselves.
But Jesus never died so people could become better performers.
He died so sinners could become new creations.
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." (2 Corinthians 5:17)
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) literally means "a new creation."
Because your goal is no longer finding someone impressed by your strengths.
Your goal becomes finding someone who will walk beside you toward Christ while fully knowing your weaknesses.
That requires a conversation almost nobody wants to have.
"What idols does your heart still fight?"
"What sins have you truly repented of?"
"What temptations return when nobody is watching?"
"What does spiritual leadership actually mean to you?"
"What wounds still influence how you love?"
"What does forgiveness look like when trust is broken?"
"What does biblical submission actually mean according to Scripture—not culture?"
"What do you fear more than obeying Christ?"
Because truthful answers might cost the relationship.
But hiding them may cost a marriage.
"Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy." (Proverbs 28:13)
The Hebrew word translated "conceals" is כָּסָה (kasah).
It literally means to cover over.
Notice Scripture never promises blessing for successful concealment.
That does not mean telling every painful detail immediately.
Biblical wisdom values discernment, timing, and appropriate boundaries.
Not every first date requires sharing every wound.

Yet intentional movement toward honesty should characterize a Christ-centered relationship. As commitment deepens, openness should deepen as well. Truth is never a weapon to shock someone, but a gift offered with humility, wisdom, and love.
"Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed." (James 5:16)
The Greek word ἐξομολογεῖσθε (exomologeisthe) means to openly acknowledge or confess.
Imagine standing at the altar promising lifelong faithfulness while carrying conversations you were too afraid to have beforehand.
Paul describes biblical love in 1 Corinthians 13.
The Greek word συγχαίρει (synchairei) means "to rejoice together."
Truth becomes something both people celebrate.
That is the difference between worldly romance and Christ-centered love.
"Will they still love me if they know?"
"Since Christ already knows everything about me and still loved me enough to die for me, why am I hiding from someone I hope to build a covenant with?"
Because Jesus Himself never pursued people through deception.
When Nathanael approached Him, Jesus exposed his heart.
When the Samaritan woman came to the well, Jesus lovingly revealed her past.
When Peter denied Him, Jesus restored rather than discarded him.
"The Word became flesh and dwelt among us... full of grace and truth." (John 1:14)
The Greek word ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen) means "pitched His tent" or "tabernacled among us."
God did not love humanity from a distance.
Likewise, healthy relationships require drawing near in truth—not merely maintaining attractive appearances from a safe distance.
That is the pattern of Christ.
He already knows every chapter of your story.
Not because your past is small.
But because His grace is greater.
This is why our theme has always been more than a slogan.
From Scandal to Grace is the story of every believer.
Peter moved from denial to restoration.
Paul moved from persecutor to apostle.
Rahab moved from prostitution to being included in the lineage of Christ.
David moved from adultery and murder to repentance and renewed fellowship with God, though not without lasting earthly consequences.
The woman caught in adultery encountered both truth and mercy.
The thief on the cross moved from condemnation to paradise.
Every testimony whispers the same truth.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
But by redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe the conversation you keep avoiding is not actually with the person you're dating.
Perhaps He has been patiently asking you to surrender the very thing you hope your future spouse never discovers.
The beautiful truth of the Gospel is this:
Nothing you confess to Christ surprises Him.
Nothing you surrender is beyond His power to redeem.
Nothing placed beneath His cross remains outside His grace.

If this article unsettled you, don't rush past that feeling. Sometimes conviction is God's mercy knocking before consequences ever arrive. Have the conversation. With God first. Then, in wisdom and appropriate timing, with the person you hope to build a covenant with. Relationships anchored in Christ are strengthened by truth spoken in love, humility, and repentance.
You may be placing biblical wisdom in front of someone before irreversible decisions are made.
Let that not be a performance for others, but a prayer before God. Your testimony may encourage someone else to step into the light of Christ.
One honest conversation today may spare years of silent sorrow tomorrow.
